newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Swiss theatre faces up to anti-Semitism.
newsitem.headline: Swiss theatre faces up to anti-Semitism.

text.p: Crowds packed a theatre in Zurich to see an unusual show tackling the sensitive issue of Swiss anti-Semitism, something particularly painful in a country still struggling to come to terms with its wartime relations with Nazi Germany.

Opening in Zurich on Monday night, the work entitled "I Don't Have Anything Against Jews, But...." will continue in other Swiss cities, putting the Holocaust centre stage by holding up an anti-Semitic mirror to Swiss society.
The performance features four actors reading real letters written by Swiss to newspapers, or addressed to private persons, followed by a panel discussion.
The letters -- a mixture of hate, twisted logic and precarious egotism -- were written over the past six months and collected by actress Shelley Kaestner, one of the four readers.
People scrabbled for last-minute tickets to a sellout one-night performance at the city's Neumarkt Theater.
The letters, whose authors were not named, offered startling views of individuals' anti-Jewish feeling.
Such sentiment has festered amid controversy over neutral Switzerland's relations with the Nazis, which have come under fierce attack from foreign critics, including Jewish groups.

Swiss efforts to make amends by setting up a fund for Holocaust victims and the Berne government's plan to revalue gold to finance humanitarian projects have raised the hackles of ultra-conservative Swiss who say their government is yielding to blackmail.
The German-speaking audience, including some from the Swiss Jewish community, packed the theatre, and extra chairs had to be brought in.
The reading began with relatively harmless, eccentric letters. One began: "As an animal rights activist, I am an anti-Semite...."
The tone grew more venomous.
Another letter, from a retired tax official, questioned why Holocaust victims needed to stash gold and assets outside Germany at all.
Some of the wealth of the Nazis' victims landed in Swiss banks which have denied charges that they are still hoarding assets of Jews who perished in the Nazi death camps.

One letter proclaimed that "hatred of the Jews doesn't just come about for no reason..." prompted appalled head-shaking. Another blamed all evils of the world -- from the atomic bomb to pornography to even Nazism itself -- on the Jews.
The letters were interspersed with Jewish jokes which grew darker and more macabre, leaving the audience stunned into silence.
Towards the end of the presentation, the four actors mingled their voices in a chorus which broke with the proclamation from one letter: "We are back! Heil Hitler!"
The reading ended with a concilliatory quote from French author Edmund Jabes, saying "If you cannot accept people different than you, there can be no real dialogue."
Kaestner, 35, who gathered the letters, told Reuters that the presentation would continue to tour Switzerland in June.
She said she had no trouble finding letters to use, adding that more than half of those she considered were negative.

"I think these people who write crass anti-Semitic letters are not able to differentiate. It doesn't concern the Jews, but rather that they need an object upon which they can discharge" their hatred, she said.

Emanuel Hurwitz, a Swiss psychoanalyst taking part in the podium discussion, said anti-Semitism has "something to do with delusions of grandeur." He added violent anti-Semitic images in the letters "require little to be set into motion again."
Jean Ziegler, an outspoken Swiss parlamentarian, said the Swiss should publish numbers on how many people trying to fleeing the Nazis were turned away at the Swiss border.
"Unless we can look in the mirror, there is no future for this land," he said.
